t:
(a) In General.—Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement under this title with the Secretary of Labor (in this title referred to as the “Secretary”). Any State which is a party to an agreement under this title may, upon providing 30 days’ written notice to the Secretary, terminate such agreement. 
    (b) Provisions of Agreement.—Any agreement under subsection (a) shall provide that the State agency of the State will make payments of emergency unemployment compensation to individuals who—
        (1) have exhausted all rights to regular compensation under the State law or under Federal law with respect to a benefit year (excluding any benefit year that ended before May 1, 2007); 
        (2) have no rights to regular compensation or extended compensation with respect to a week under such law or any other State unemployment compensation law or to compensation under any other Federal law (except as provided under subsection (e)); and 
        (3) are not receiving compensation with respect to such week under the unemployment compensation law of Canada.  
    (c) Exhaustion of Benefits.—For purposes of subsection (b)(1), an individual shall be deemed to have exhausted such individual’s rights to regular compensation under a State law when—
        (1) no payments of regular compensation can be made under such law because such individual has received all regular compensation available to such individual based on employment or wages during such individual’s base period; or 
        (2) such individual’s rights to such compensation have been terminated by reason of the expiration of the benefit year with respect to which such rights existed.  
    (d) Weekly Benefit Amount, Etc.—For purposes of any agreement under this title—
        (1) the amount of emergency unemployment compensation which shall be payable to any individual for any week of total unemployment shall be equal to the amount of the regular compensation (including dependents’ allowances) payable to such individual during such individual’s benefit year under the State law for a week of total unemployment; 
        (2) the terms and conditions of the State law which apply to claims for regular compensation and to the payment thereof shall apply to claims for emergency unemployment compensation and the payment thereof, except—
            (A) that an individual shall not be eligible for emergency unemployment compensation under this title unless, in the base period with respect to which the individual exhausted all rights to regular compensation under the State law, the individual had 20 weeks of full-time insured employment or the equivalent in insured wages, as determined under the provisions of the State law implementing section 202(a)(5) of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970 (26 U.S.C. 3304 note); and 
            (B) where otherwise inconsistent with the provisions of this title or with the regulations or operating instructions of the Secretary promulgated to carry out this title; and  
        (3) the maximum amount of emergency unemployment compensation payable to any individual for whom an emergency unemployment compensation account is established under section 4002 shall not exceed the amount established in such account for such individual.  
    (e) Election by States.—Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal law (and if State law permits), the Governor of a State that is in an extended benefit period may provide for the payment of emergency unemployment compensation prior to extended compensation to individuals who otherwise meet the requirements of this section. 
    (f) Unauthorized Aliens Ineligible.—A State shall require as a condition of eligibility for emergency unemployment compensation under this Act that each alien who receives such compensation must be legally authorized to work in the United States, as defined for purposes of the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (26 U.S.C. 3301 et seq.). In determining whether an alien meets the requirements of this subsection, a State must follow the procedures provided in section 1137(d) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1320b–7(d)).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a State "participat[ing] in an agreement" with the Secretary is outside-party participation, but the agreement is simply a State opting in to administer a federal benefit program under terms fixed by statute. The State is not consulted on, or invited to comment on, any federal decision. The passing mention of the Secretary's "regulations or operating instructions" does not require rulemaking, a comment period, a hearing, an advisory body, or a right to sue.
fable.s: Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement under this title with the Secretary of Labor

qwen_block.w: This section describes the administration of unemployment benefits by States under a federal agreement. The definition explicitly excludes 'applications for benefits or grants' and focuses on consultation/coordination *before* a federal decision is made. Here, the 'participation' refers to the State's role in administering the benefit program, not a consultative process in federal policy-making or decision-making. The federal decision (the statute) is already established; the State is merely implementing it.
qwen_block.s: Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement under this title with the Secretary of Labor... Any agreement under subsection (a) shall provide that the State agency of the State will make payments of emergency unemployment compensation to individuals
qwen_block.b:
To determine the label, I must analyze whether the section involves participation by parties outside the federal government in a federal decision-making process.

1.  **Analyze the Actors and Actions:**
    *   Subsection (a) states: "Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement under this title with the Secretary of Labor..."
    *   Subsection (b) details the provisions of this agreement, specifically that the State agency will make payments to individuals.
    *   Subsections (c), (d), (e), and (f) define eligibility, benefit amounts, and conditions for these payments.

2.  **Evaluate against the Definition:**
    *   The definition states: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
    *   It explicitly excludes: "applications for benefits or grants."
    *   It also excludes: "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies or federal officials."

3.  **Determine the Nature of the Interaction:**
    *   The text describes a mechanism for States to administer unemployment compensation programs using federal funds or under federal guidelines.
    *   The "agreement" mentioned is essentially a grant or cooperative agreement where the State agrees to administer benefits according to federal rules.
    *   The "participation" mentioned in subsection (a) refers to the State's participation in the *program* (i.e., administering benefits), not participation in the *federal decision-making process* (e.g., rulemaking, advisory boards, public hearings).
    *   The definition explicitly says: "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." While this is an agreement to administer benefits, it falls under the umbrella of benefit administration/grant-like structures rather than public participation in policy decisions. The State is not consulting with the Secretary to *make* a decision; the State is agreeing to *implement* a program defined by the statute.
    *   Furthermore, the "decision" being made here is whether an individual gets benefits, which is an administrative determination, not a policy decision involving public consultation. The State's role is operational.

4.  **Check for "Tempting but Wrong" readings:**
    *   *Temptation:* The word "participate" appears in subsection (a).
    *   *Why it fails:* The definition warns against mere appearance of words like "participation" in proper nouns or boilerplate without actual outside-party process in decision-making. Here, "participate in an agreement" means joining a program, not engaging in a consultative process for a federal decision. The State is an administrator, not a consultant on policy.
    *   *Temptation:* States are outside the government.
    *   *Why it fails:* While States are outside entities, the interaction described is the administration of benefits (excluded) or the execution of a pre-defined statutory agreement, not a consultation *before* a federal decision is made. The federal decision (the law itself) is already made. The agreement is the implementation vehicle.

5.  **Conclusion:** This section describes the administration of unemployment benefits by States under federal law. It does not describe a process where the federal government consults with outsiders *before* making a decision. It describes the terms of a benefit program. Therefore, it is "No".

opus.w: The section assumes the Secretary will issue regulations to carry out this title, and the definition counts authority to issue regulations as participation (see Example 6). The tempting basis for 'Yes' is that states 'participate in an agreement,' but that is opting into a program, like a grant or contract, rather than being consulted on a federal decision. So the rulemaking reference, not the state agreements, is what supports the label.
opus.s: where otherwise inconsistent with the provisions of this title or with the regulations or operating instructions of the Secretary promulgated to carry out this title
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading:** States "enter into and participate in an agreement" with the Secretary of Labor, so states seem to be outsiders taking part. That fails against the definition. Opting into a payment agreement is like signing up for a federal program or contract. It doesn't consult states before a federal decision, so on its own it isn't participation.
2. **What actually decides it:** The section refers to "the regulations or operating instructions of the Secretary promulgated to carry out this title." This assumes the Secretary will make regulations under this title. Under the definition and Example 6, giving an agency authority to issue regulations counts as participation, because rulemaking brings in public comment. This is only a passing reference, not a direct grant of rulemaking power, so my confidence is moderate.

qwen_chat.w: The section describes a voluntary agreement between a State and the Secretary of Labor to administer emergency unemployment compensation. This is analogous to a grant or contract application, which the definition explicitly excludes from participation. There is no requirement for the federal government to consult with outside parties before making a decision; rather, the State opts into the program.
qwen_chat.s: Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement under this title with the Secretary of Labor
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: The section uses the word "participate" in subsection (a) ("Any State which desires to do so may enter into and participate in an agreement..."), which might suggest participation. However, the definition explicitly states that "applications for benefits or grants" are not participation, and entering into an agreement to administer a benefit program is functionally similar to applying for or accepting a grant/contract. Furthermore, the "participation" here is the State's role in administering a federal program, not a process where the federal government consults with outsiders *before* making a decision. The decision to enter the agreement is voluntary by the State, and the subsequent actions are administrative. The definition's trap regarding "applications for benefits" and the lack of a pre-decision consultation mechanism with outsiders (the State is the partner, not an outside consultant in the advisory sense) points to "No".

Wait, let's re-read the definition carefully. "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
Subsection (a) says a State *may* enter into an agreement. This is not the federal government consulting with the State before a decision. It is the State opting in.
Subsection (e) says the Governor *may* provide for payment.
There is no requirement for the Secretary to consult with the State or public before making a decision. The State applies/opts in.
The definition says: "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." Entering an agreement to receive federal funds for unemployment compensation is akin to a grant application or contract.
Therefore, the answer is No.
